questions.question: How would you explain the role of glycogen in physical activity? / [CO1]
questions.solution_html:
• How would you explain the role of glycogen in physical activity?
  • Glycogen is a stored form of carbohydrate found mainly in the liver and
  • muscles.(1 mark) During physical activity, the body breaks down glycogen
  • into glucose, which is used by muscle cells to produce energy. This process
  • is especially important during moderate to high-intensity exercise, where the
  • demand for energy increases rapidly. Muscle glycogen provides a quick and
  • accessible energy source, helping to maintain performance and delay
  • fatigue. As exercise continues, glycogen stores become depleted, which can
  • lead to a drop in energy levels and reduced endurance. Therefore, adequate
  • glycogen storage is essential for optimal athletic performance and
  • recovery.(4 marks)
  • [A] / [CO1]

questions.question: Explain the importance of MSA in identifying conserved protein domains. / [CO4]
questions.solution_html:
• Explain the importance of MSA in identifying conserved protein
  • domains.
  • Multiple Sequence Alignment (MSA) is important for identifying
  • conserved protein domains because it compares amino acid sequences
  • from different proteins or species. By aligning these sequences, MSA
  • highlights regions that are highly similar or unchanged (conserved),
  • suggesting they have important structural or functional roles. Conserved
  • domains often indicate shared ancestry and are crucial for the protein’s
  • function, such as binding or catalytic activity. Identifying these domains
  • helps in predicting protein function, understanding evolution, and guiding
  • drug design or genetic research. (5 marks)

questions.question: Compare sequence databases and structure databases with examples. / [CO3]
questions.solution_html:
• Compare sequence databases and structure databases with examples.
  • The sequence databases and structure databases are both essential tools
  • for storing and organizing biological information.Sequence databases store
  • information about the linear sequence of nucleotides or amino acids,
  • structure databases contain data about the three-dimensional shapes of
  • biomolecules, especially proteins and nucleic acids.(3 marks) Sequence
  • databases store nucleotide or protein sequences, which are linear, and are
  • primarily used for sequence alignment, gene prediction, and evolutionary
  • studies. They focus on the order of nucleotides or amino acids in a
  • sequence. Examples of sequence databases include GenBank, UniProt, and
  • EMBL. These databases rely on sequence-based techniques, such as DNA
  • sequencing, to gather data and are commonly applied in genomic studies,
  • functional annotations, and mutation analysis. structure databases contain
  • 3D coordinates of atoms in molecules, providing detailed information about
  • molecular shapes, folding, and interactions. They are used for visualizing
  • and analyzing the three-dimensional structures of biomolecules. Examples
  • of structure databases include the Protein Data Bank (PDB), ModBase, and
  • SCOP. Structure databases rely on experimental methods like X-ray
  • crystallography and NMR spectroscopy, as well as computational modeling,
  • to determine 3D structures. These databases are mainly applied in drug
  • design, protein interaction studies, and molecular modeling.(7 marks)
  • [A] / [CO3]

  • details. The tool can depict molecular features such as secondary structures
